source.title: Investigating the Impact of Model Width and Density on Generalization in Presence of Label Noise
source.authors: Yihao Xue; Kyle Whitecross; Baharan Mirzasoleiman

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some plotted values are figure-only.
record.tranche_reason: Width sweeps show that label noise and regularization can produce a final rise in test loss, qualifying the claim that wider networks keep improving.
record.gate_note: The paper studies label noise and test loss across width and density. Optimizer and batch-size details are experimental setup, not comparative results. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study investigates a related width–generalization claim, but its recorded outcomes concern test loss under noisy labels, without establishing the width needed for zero training error. These results do not establish whether classification test error keeps falling beyond interpolation as V2 specifies. Accuracy plots are included, but their curve values and interpolation status cannot be established from the supplied text.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors report final ascent in test loss across width and density, its amplification by stronger regularization and robust methods, and benefits from intermediate density and wider sparse models. The sample-size qualification needs care: their finite-dimensional regression experiments also show that increasing sample size can initially enable final ascent when n/d is small, before alleviating it in other regimes.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines noisy-label regression theory and neural-network classification, rather than fitting fixed random labels or measuring natural-label generalization against chance. It sweeps width, density, noise, and regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported width outcome changes with noise level and type, training-set size, regularization strength, dataset, and robust training method.

fits_no_version.finding: Under sufficiently strong label noise, test loss can reach its minimum at intermediate widths. Regularization and robust methods can accentuate this advantage, while larger samples alleviate final ascent in the reported neural-network comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With noisy training labels, increasing model width can eventually raise clean-label test loss, depending on regularization, sample size and noise distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Intermediate density can improve noisy-label generalization; adjusting density can attain lower loss than adjusting weight decay, and wider sparse models can outperform denser models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Randomly fixing an appropriate fraction of weights to zero can improve generalization under label noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Label noise reverses the reported relationship between width and function-complexity proxies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing width can decrease measured function complexity with clean labels but increase it with noisy labels.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence
record.problems: Many width-sweep outcomes are shown only in plots; the text gives qualitative trends rather than numeric test-loss values. Theoretical results use random-feature ridge regression and asymptotic assumptions; neural-network experiments concern noisy training labels and clean test labels.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every plotted dataset, noise fraction, and width curve were transcribed where the text does not give a distinct qualitative result. Figures 6–9, 10–12, 20, and 29–32 contain additional plotted conditions; no precise values were reconstructed from the figures. R8 is retained only to mark that the cited Cars density figures do not establish a width result.

untested.parts: Matched natural-label and fixed-random-label training fits and held-out accuracy relative to chance.
Classification test-error trends beyond a demonstrated zero-training-error threshold, under the specified converged, unregularized training conditions.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity or convolutional initialization.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons with fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to the training recipe.
Dropout comparisons; permanently masking weights to change density is not dropout.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally sized random subsets and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The paper explicitly disputes a broad larger-models-always-generalize-better interpretation. That is broader than V2's stated classification-error result beyond interpolation. The extracted plot text provides axes and captions rather than recoverable curve coordinates; no accuracy trend was inferred from axis labels. Additional plotted conditions are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: No fixed random-label memorization comparison against natural labels.

Does not establish the width needed to reach zero training error or test the stated MNIST/downsampled CIFAR-10 setup without explicit regularization. Its experiments focus on noisy training labels and clean test labels.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
The paper measures function-complexity proxies, not magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps.

rows.subject: two-layer linear network with a random first layer
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical width sweep for ridge regression with label noise; test risk curve evaluated asymptotically.
rows.measure: Expected test risk (test loss) versus width.
rows.value: Risk finds its minimum at an intermediate width under sufficiently large κ; the curve can ascend at large widths.
rows.note: The result is theoretical and concerns noisy training labels with clean test labels.
rows.check: The final ascent is supported for regularized random-feature regression risk. This does not measure V2's classification test error beyond zero training error. The regularizer is λ = (n/d)λ0, not n×d×λ0.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU networks
rows.size_stated: width controlled by number of hidden neurons; exact sizes not stated in result text
rows.operation_detail: Test-loss width sweep under symmetric label noise on MNIST with MSE loss.

conditions.value: final ascent occurs at a noise threshold; as low as 20% in reported experiments

rows.baseline: λ = 0: double descent reported for the comparison in the figure
rows.value: With λ = 0.001, final ascent is reported; stronger regularization makes it more pronounced and reduces the required noise level.
rows.note: The paper says the final ascent occurs when noise reaches a threshold; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Reports MSE test loss, without identifying interpolation or establishing a corresponding classification-error ascent. MNIST models use 1/20 of the training data for these measurements. Split regularization and noise conditions into separate rows; the comparison does not have one uniform outcome.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.size_stated: width controlled by convolutional filters; exact sizes not stated in result text
rows.operation_detail: Test-loss width sweep under symmetric label noise on CIFAR-10 with MSE loss.
rows.baseline: At λ = 0.0005 and 20% noise, double descent is reported.
rows.value: At λ = 0.001 and 20% noise, final ascent is reported; stronger regularization exacerbates it.
rows.note: Other plotted loss curves are not assigned precise values.
rows.check: The stated loss comparison is correct, but MSE ascent does not establish classification-error ascent beyond interpolation. These measurements use 1/5 of CIFAR-10. Separate the λ = 0.0005 double-descent condition from the λ = 0.001 final-ascent condition.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.size_stated: width controlled by convolutional filters; exact sizes not stated in result text
rows.operation_detail: Test-loss width sweep with symmetric versus asymmetric label noise.
rows.baseline: With symmetric noise, final ascent is absent.
rows.value: With asymmetric noise, final ascent is present.
rows.note: The paper says this trend is not obvious on CIFAR-100, possibly because its noise generation is less skewed.
rows.check: The symmetric/asymmetric comparison concerns CE test loss on full CIFAR-10, without an interpolation measurement. Separate the two noise conditions. Absence of final ascent alone does not establish V2's continued improvement.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU networks
rows.size_stated: width controlled by number of hidden neurons; exact sizes not stated in result text
rows.operation_detail: Test-loss width sweep while varying training-set fraction.
rows.baseline: With 1/20 of the original data, final ascent occurs.
rows.value: With 1/2 of the original data, final ascent is not observed.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative comparison; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: The sample-size comparison is supported for MSE loss, but does not establish V2. Separate sample fractions: final ascent at 1/20 and its absence at 1/2 are distinct outcomes, not one partial effect.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.size_stated: width controlled by convolutional filters; exact sizes not stated in result text
rows.operation_detail: Test-loss width sweep while varying training-set fraction.
rows.baseline: With 1/20 of the original data, final ascent occurs.
rows.value: With 1/5 of the original data, final ascent is not observed.
rows.note: The text reports the qualitative comparison; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: This experiment uses CE loss. Separate sample fractions rather than assigning a partial state to the comparison. Neither interpolation status nor classification-error trends are established by the recorded loss outcomes.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.size_stated: width controlled by convolutional filters; exact sizes not stated in result text
rows.operation_detail: Test-loss width sweep under noisy labels using ELR.
rows.baseline: Without ELR, final ascent is not observed on CIFAR-10 under 60% symmetric noise with 1/5 of the data.
rows.value: With ELR, final ascent occurs under 40% symmetric noise on the full data.
rows.note: The study describes robust algorithms as amplifying the final ascent.
rows.check: ELR final ascent is reported, but this row records loss rather than a readable accuracy trend beyond interpolation. Its baseline also changes noise level, sample size and training recipe, so it is not a matched estimate of ELR's effect.

rows.subject: InceptionResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Test-loss width sweep on web-labeled Red Stanford Cars.
rows.value: The paper reports a final-ascent effect for density in the dataset, but does not state a width-sweep result here.
rows.note: No width result is described in text for this model; density results are not a width measure.
rows.check: Remove as a width-result row. The authors explicitly vary density because varying InceptionResNet-v2 width is difficult. Figures 10 and 32 contain density experiments, including a separate ELR condition.

rows.subject: ResNet34
rows.operation_detail: Compared test loss across density and weight-decay settings.

conditions.value: vary λ at density 1 versus vary density at λ′ = 0.0005

rows.baseline: Varying weight decay also produces a U-shaped loss curve.
rows.value: Density variation produces a U-shaped curve whose bottom is lower than the weight-decay curve.
rows.note: This compares density with regularization; it does not directly test the version's width claim.
rows.check: Correctly describes a density-versus-weight-decay loss comparison at fixed width; it does not test V2.

rows.subject: CNN on CIFAR-10 DOG vs AIRPLANE
rows.size_stated: two convolutional layers; fully connected ReLU layer size 384; width set by convolutional channels
rows.operation_detail: Measured trajectory length and variance of first-layer bias across width under clean versus noisy labels.
rows.measure: Trajectory length and variance of first-layer bias as function-complexity proxies.
rows.baseline: At 0% noise, both quantities decrease as width increases.
rows.value: At 40% noise, both quantities increase as width increases.
rows.note: These are complexity proxies, not measures named in the claim versions.
rows.check: Trajectory length and bias variance are function-complexity proxies, not outcomes named by any version.

rows.subject: CNN on CIFAR-10 DOG vs AIRPLANE
rows.size_stated: two convolutional layers; fully connected ReLU layer size 384; width set by convolutional channels
rows.operation_detail: Measured product of layer-wise spectral norms at the final epoch across width under clean versus noisy labels.
rows.baseline: At 0% noise, spectral norm decreases as width increases.
rows.value: At 40% noise, spectral norm increases as width increases.
rows.note: This is a complexity proxy, not magnitude-aware sharpness or a direct gap measure.
rows.check: Spectral-norm products do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its association with generalization gaps.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Noisy-label settings with sufficiently large noise, and stronger regularization
reader_labels.reason: Width sweeps report final ascent in test loss at larger widths, including its appearance with stronger regularization (R1–R4, R7). This challenges continued test-error improvement in those settings.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Training-set size and noise type vary
reader_labels.reason: The ascent is absent in some reported comparisons with more data or symmetric noise, while appearing with smaller samples or asymmetric noise (R4–R6).
